title: Lua tutorial: tables, functions, metatables and errors — cv.cm
description: Learn Lua step by step: run Hello, world, local variables and types, loops, functions and closures, tables, metatables, OOP and pcall error handling.
answer: Lua is a lightweight, embeddable scripting language used in games, Roblox (through its Luau dialect), Neovim, Redis and embedded devices. It has a small syntax and a single data structure, the table, which serves as array, dictionary and object. This page covers installing Lua, variables and types, control flow, functions, tables, metatables, error handling with pcall and a complete example.

sections.h: What Lua is and what it is used for
body: Lua is a small, fast, dynamically typed scripting language created in 1993 at PUC-Rio, a university in Brazil. Its whole interpreter is a compact library written in C, which makes it easy to embed inside larger programs. It has one data structure, the table, and very few concepts, so it is quick to learn.

Lua is mostly used as an embedded scripting language: game engines and games (Roblox uses a Lua dialect called Luau; LÖVE and Defold use Lua), the Neovim editor, the Redis database, network tools such as Nginx with OpenResty, and many embedded devices. LuaJIT is a popular just-in-time compiler for Lua 5.1 code.

sections.h: Install Lua and run Hello, world
body: Install Lua with your package manager (for example `brew install lua` or `apt install lua5.4`) or build it from the source at lua.org. Run `lua` alone for an interactive prompt.
Comments start with `--`. A block comment is written `--[[ ... ]]`. Statements do not need semicolons.
Variables are global by default. Always declare them with `local` unless you really mean a global. Lua has eight basic types; the ones you use every day are below.

body.code:
local name = "Lua"
local year = 1993              -- integer
local pi = 3.14159             -- float
local ok = true
local nothing = nil

print(type(name), type(year), type(nothing))  -- string  number  nil
print(math.type(year), math.type(pi))         -- integer  float
print(name .. " " .. year)                    -- Lua 1993 (.. joins strings)
print(#name)                                  -- 3 (length)
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, 2 ^ 10)           -- 3.5  3  1  1024.0
print(string.format("%.2f", pi))              -- 3.14
print(tonumber("42") + 1, tostring(10))       -- 43  10

body: The not-equal operator is `~=`, not `!=`. Logical operators are the words `and`, `or` and `not`.
Blocks end with the keyword `end`. Lua has `if`/`elseif`/`else`, `while`, `repeat ... until`, a numeric `for` and a generic `for` that works with iterators.

body.code:
local score = 72
if score >= 90 then
  print("A")
elseif score >= 70 then
  print("B")                   -- B
else
  print("C")
end

for i = 1, 3 do                -- 1 to 3, inclusive
  io.write(i, " ")             -- 1 2 3
end
print()

for i = 10, 1, -4 do io.write(i, " ") end   -- 10 6 2
print()

local n = 3
while n > 0 do n = n - 1 end

repeat
  n = n + 1
until n >= 2
print(n)                       -- 2

body: There is no `continue` statement; use `goto continue` with a `::continue::` label, or restructure the loop with an `if`.
Functions are values. They can take a variable number of arguments with `...` and return multiple values. Closures capture local variables from the enclosing scope.

body.code:
local function add(a, b)
  return a + b
end

local function minmax(t)
  local lo, hi = math.huge, -math.huge
  for _, v in ipairs(t) do
    lo, hi = math.min(lo, v), math.max(hi, v)
  end
  return lo, hi                -- two return values
end

local function counter()
  local count = 0
  return function()            -- a closure
    count = count + 1
    return count
  end
end

print(add(2, 3))               -- 5
local lo, hi = minmax({4, 9, 1})
print(lo, hi)                  -- 1  9
local next_id = counter()
print(next_id(), next_id())    -- 1  2
local function sum(...)
  local total = 0
  for _, v in ipairs({...}) do total = total + v end
  return total
end
print(sum(1, 2, 3))            -- 6

body: A table is an associative array that can be indexed by any value except `nil`. The same structure serves as an array, a dictionary, a set, a module or an object. By convention arrays start at index 1.

body.code:
local fruits = {"apple", "banana"}
table.insert(fruits, "cherry")
print(#fruits, fruits[1])            -- 3  apple

for i, f in ipairs(fruits) do        -- array part, in order
  print(i, f)
end

local ages = {ann = 31, bo = 25}
ages["cy"] = 40
ages.bo = nil                        -- remove a key
for k, v in pairs(ages) do           -- all keys, order not defined
  print(k, v)
end

table.sort(fruits, function(a, b) return a > b end)
print(table.concat(fruits, ", "))    -- cherry, banana, apple

body.note: Indexes start at 1, and `#t` is only reliable for sequences without holes. Setting `t[2] = nil` in the middle of an array makes the length undefined; use `table.remove(t, 2)` to delete and shift elements instead.

body: Metatables are Lua's signature feature. A metatable attached to a table changes how it behaves: `__index` supplies missing keys (used for inheritance), and fields such as `__add`, `__eq` and `__tostring` overload operators. The colon syntax `obj:method()` passes the object as the hidden first parameter `self`.

Lua also has coroutines (`coroutine.create`, `coroutine.resume`, `coroutine.yield`), which let a function pause and resume later. Game scripts often use them for step-by-step behavior that spans several frames.

Raise an error with `error(message)`. Catch it with `pcall` (protected call), which returns `false` plus the error instead of stopping the program. Many library functions return `nil` and an error message instead of raising an error, as `io.open` does.

body.code:
local function divide(a, b)
  if b == 0 then
    error("division by zero")
  end
  return a / b
end

local ok, result = pcall(divide, 10, 2)
print(ok, result)                  -- true  5.0

ok, result = pcall(divide, 1, 0)
print(ok, result)                  -- false  script.lua:3: division by zero

local f, err = io.open("missing.txt", "r")
if not f then print("open failed: " .. err) end

body: The file name and line number in the error message depend on where the code runs. `assert(value, message)` raises an error when `value` is `false` or `nil` and is a short way to check results.

sections.h: A small complete program: word count
body: This program counts words in a text with a pattern match, sorts them by frequency and prints the top three. It uses string patterns, tables, sorting with a custom comparator and string formatting.

body.code:
local text = [[
The cat and the dog. The dog sat,
and the cat ran.
]]

local counts = {}
for word in text:lower():gmatch("%a+") do
  counts[word] = (counts[word] or 0) + 1
end

local list = {}
for word, n in pairs(counts) do
  list[#list + 1] = {word = word, n = n}
end
table.sort(list, function(a, b)
  if a.n ~= b.n then return a.n > b.n end
  return a.word < b.word
end)

for i = 1, 3 do
  print(string.format("%-4s %d", list[i].word, list[i].n))
end
-- the  4
-- and  2
-- cat  2

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: forgetting `local` and creating globals by accident; using `!=` instead of `~=`; expecting arrays to start at 0; using `.` instead of `:` when calling methods (`obj.method()` does not pass `self`); and assuming `pairs` returns keys in a fixed order.

faq.q: Why do Lua arrays start at 1?
faq.a: Lua's designers chose 1-based indexing to match common mathematical and non-programmer conventions. The standard library functions such as `ipairs`, `#` and `table.insert` all assume sequences start at 1.
The standard Lua interpreter is small and generally fast for a dynamic language, and LuaJIT is much faster for many workloads. Actual speed depends on the task, so measure your own case.

faq.q: What is the difference between pairs and ipairs?
faq.a: `ipairs` walks the array part in order from index 1 until the first `nil`. `pairs` visits every key in the table in an unspecified order.
Luau is a language derived from Lua 5.1 and developed by Roblox. It adds gradual typing and performance improvements and is used for Roblox games.

Yes. It has a small, consistent syntax and few concepts, which is why it is popular for game modding and teaching. Its minimal standard library means you rely on the host program or modules for more features.
